How this list is ordered

Four gates, applied in this order to every published US record. There is no score and no weighting — each gate either separates two machines or hands them to the next one.

  1. 1 Does it run the set?

    Every record is put through the compatibility engine against all of the loads at once — running watts against continuous output, the worst start-up instant against the surge ceiling, waveform where a load demands one. Green first, then the tight fits, then anything the engine could not read, then the machines that cannot do it. A machine that cannot start the load in front of it is not a cheaper option.

  2. 2 Can we prove how long?

    A runtime is only printed where the brand publishes what it takes to compute one — a usable-capacity coefficient, whether stated as depth of discharge and inverter efficiency or as one combined figure — and never from the number on the box. Records that reach the target sort first, records with a proven but shorter figure next (longest first: inside that band none of them does the job, so the one that gets closest wins), and records whose duration cannot be proven at all sort last inside their verdict band. That is a statement about published data, not about the hardware, and each of those rows says so.

  3. 3 Can it be bought today?

    A record under a verified out-of-stock policy, or one we may not sell into your state, sorts behind an equivalent one that can be bought. It stays on the list with the reason attached rather than disappearing. Whether WattPair happens to hold a purchase link for a record is not part of this gate and never moves it: a machine we cannot link to is ranked exactly as if we could, and simply carries no buy button.

  4. 4 Then price.

    Cheapest first, inside everything above. One mains standard and one currency per page, so every comparison is like for like. A record with no verified price sorts to the back of its own band — the absence of a price is not a low price.

The loads this ranks against

One diesel air heater, on its own, at 34 W. That is the manufacturer’s own figure for its highest setting on a 2.2 kW-of-heat unit — the electricity runs a fan and a fuel pump, the heat comes out of the fuel tank, and the ratio of heat out to electricity in is somewhere between sixty and a hundred to one. It is the least intuitive number in this library and it is the reason this page exists: people size a power station for a heater and get an answer two orders of magnitude too large. Two things this ranking does NOT tell you, stated here rather than left to be discovered. The start-up draw is 100 W, but it is held for a minute or two while the glow plug lights the fuel, so it is checked against continuous output rather than against a surge rating — the caveat under the load table says so. And this is a 12/24 V DC appliance: most people wire it to a station’s DC output, where the real limit is that port’s own current rating, not the inverter this page ranks. The ranking below is the conservative reading, through the AC path.

Twelve hours — one cold night, run continuously, which is what this appliance is for. The manufacturer’s own table shows the draw falling to 23, 12, 8 and 4 W as the heat setting drops, so a night spent on a lower setting lasts proportionally longer than anything below; this page takes the highest setting throughout, which is the conservative end of a four-fold range rather than a typical one.

The start-up figure here is not a spike, and is judged more strictly

100 W is what this load draws while it is starting, and it holds that draw for 60 to 125 seconds — long enough that a station's surge rating, which describes an event lasting a second or two, does not apply to it at all. So it is not added to the start-up total above. It is checked against continuous output instead, for the whole of that time, which is the harder of the two tests rather than an exemption from one.

Why 5 records rank below machines they out-spec

5 of the 12 records here start and hold this load set and still rank below machines they out-spec, for one reason: we have found no depth of discharge and no inverter efficiency published by EcoFlow for them, so the hours a reader actually wants cannot be computed from anything but the number on the box — and dividing a nameplate by a load is the one thing this site will not do. The other side of that is BLUETTI and Jackery: they are the only brands here that publish both, which is the whole reason every proven runtime above belongs to them. The rule rewarded disclosure, not hardware.

What their rows do carry is the bound: that record’s nameplate over this set’s average draw of 34 W, which is arithmetic anyone can redo against the summary above — floored, never rounded up, so the printed ceiling never claims an hour more than the number supports — and it is printed on every one of those rows. But it is a ceiling and not a duration: it assumes the pack surrenders every watt-hour printed on it and that the inverter loses nothing turning DC into AC, and no battery does either. The real hours sit somewhere below that ceiling, and the two missing figures are exactly what would say how far below. That is the difference between a number this page will print and a number it will not.

The scope of that finding, stated: as of 2026-08-08 we read each manufacturer’s own published documents for these 5 models and found no depth-of-discharge and no inverter-efficiency figure in them. It is a statement about what those documents contained on that date — not a claim that the number exists nowhere. Send us one that is published and the record moves, and the row moves with it. This is a statement about published data, not about the hardware — the verdict column judges that separately, and it comes first.

The load that changes the answer

Add a 12V portable fridge/freezer to the same set and the first gate is still a formality: 12 of the 12 still clear it outright, against 12 on the set above. The reason is one instant: a 12V portable fridge/freezer asks for 180 W at start-up on its own, against 34 W for everything on the list above put together. There is no locked-rotor rating behind that figure to quote: the compressor runs at variable speed, its own inverter board ramps it up rather than throwing it across the line, and its data sheet carries no locked-rotor column at all. Which is the ranking of these two loads that people get backwards: the cool box is the bigger electrical load of the pair, by a factor of nearly three, and it is the one that decides how long the night lasts. The heater is a rounding error next to it. The quiz carries this set as a preset.

Questions people ask about this list

Do all 12 of them really run it?
On this set, yes — and that is the finding, not a formality. 34 W of running draw and 34 W at the worst start-up instant is inside every published US record's ceilings, so not one of them is ruled out on electrical grounds. Which means the buying question is not “will it run a diesel air heater” — it is “how long”, and that is where these machines stop being interchangeable.
